questions.question: What is Apache Maven and what is 'convention over configuration'?
questions.title: What Is Maven?
questions.direct_answer: Maven is a build and dependency management tool for Java that uses 'convention over configuration' — follow the standard directory structure and Maven works with minimal setup, without explicitly configuring every step.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core understanding of Maven's design philosophy — 'convention over configuration' is a frequently asked concept
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing Maven only as 'a dependency management tool' — it's a full build lifecycle tool
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast with Gradle's more flexible approach and explain when Maven's convention is an advantage vs. a constraint

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Apache Maven is an open-source build and project management tool for Java. It does two things really well: manages your build lifecycle (compile, test, package, deploy) and manages your dependencies (downloading and resolving all the JAR files your project needs). The key design principle Maven introduced is 'convention over configuration'. In older tools like Ant, you had to explicitly configure every step — where are your source files, where should compiled classes go, how should tests be run. Maven says: if everyone follows the same standard structure, you barely need any configuration at all. If you put your Java source code in src/main/java, your tests in src/test/java, and your resources in src/main/resources — Maven just knows where everything is and works without you telling it. You override conventions only when you actually need to deviate. This dramatically reduces boilerplate configuration. The trade-off is reduced flexibility — you're expected to follow Maven's conventions, and deviating from them can be painful.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Maven is a build lifecycle + dependency management tool for Java
Convention over configuration: standard project structure means minimal configuration needed
Standard structure: src/main/java (code), src/test/java (tests), src/main/resources (configs)
Build output goes to target/ directory by default
Declared in pom.xml (Project Object Model) — the single config file for a Maven project

sections.hook: Maven does two jobs: manage your build lifecycle and manage your dependencies. Its big idea is that following conventions beats writing configuration.

beats.content: Before Maven, you'd write an Ant XML file that explicitly said 'compile these files, put the output here, run these tests.' Every project had different conventions. Maven flipped that. It says: put your code in src/main/java, your tests in src/test/java, your resources in src/main/resources — and Maven just knows what to do. No configuration needed for the happy path.

That's convention over configuration. Follow the standard, get the behavior for free. Deviate from the standard, and you have to configure your way out. Most Spring Boot projects never deviate, so a five-line pom.xml with just GAV coordinates and a parent gets you a fully working build.

beats.label: What Maven manages for you:
items: Build lifecycle: validate, compile, test, package, install, deploy
Dependency resolution: downloads JARs from Maven Central, caches locally
Plugin execution: compiler, surefire for tests, spring-boot repackage

beats.content: sharp edge: convention over configuration is a two-edged sword. It's incredibly productive until you need to do something non-standard. Then XML config gets verbose fast. That's where Gradle's flexibility wins.

sections.cap: Maven is opinionated by design. Follow its conventions and you get a working build with almost no config. The pom.xml just declares what your project is — Maven handles the how.

questions.question: What are Maven coordinates and what do groupId, artifactId, and version mean?
questions.title: Maven Coordinates: groupId, artifactId, version (GAV)
questions.direct_answer: Maven coordinates uniquely identify an artifact: groupId is the organization (e.g., org.springframework), artifactId is the specific module name (e.g., spring-core), and version is the release version — together written as groupId:artifactId:version.

interviewer_intent.testing: Fundamental Maven knowledge — GAV coordinates appear in every pom.xml and every dependency declaration
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing groupId and artifactId — groupId is the organization/package namespace, artifactId is the specific artifact
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that GAV coordinates are how Maven prevents collisions — two different organizations can have artifacts with the same name as long as their groupIds differ

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven uses three coordinates together — sometimes called GAV — to uniquely identify any artifact in the Maven ecosystem. GroupId is like the organization or namespace, typically a reversed domain name similar to Java package conventions. For example, 'org.springframework' or 'com.google.guava' or 'com.example' for your own company. ArtifactId is the name of the specific project or module within that group. So 'org.springframework' has artifactIds like 'spring-core', 'spring-web', 'spring-context' — each a distinct module. Version is exactly what it sounds like — '5.3.21', '3.0.0', and so on. Together, groupId:artifactId:version uniquely identifies one specific JAR in the entire Maven Central repository. When you declare a dependency in pom.xml, you're writing these three coordinates. Maven uses them to locate the exact JAR in the repository, download it, and add it to your classpath. The GAV model is what enables Maven's central repository to work — it's a globally unique addressing system for Java artifacts.

sections.title: Key Points
content: groupId: organization/namespace — e.g., 'org.springframework', 'com.example'
artifactId: specific module name — e.g., 'spring-web', 'my-service'
version: specific release — e.g., '3.2.0', '2.7.18-SNAPSHOT'
GAV together uniquely identifies any artifact in Maven Central
Written in pom.xml and in dependency declarations: <groupId>, <artifactId>, <version>

sections.hook: Every JAR in the Java world has a three-part address. GAV coordinates are how Maven finds exactly the right library, every time.

beats.label: The three parts:
items: groupId: the organization namespace, like a reversed domain (org.springframework, com.google.guava)
artifactId: the specific module within that group (spring-web, spring-context, guava)
version: the exact release (3.2.0, 2.7.18-SNAPSHOT)

beats.content: Together they form a globally unique address: org.springframework:spring-web:6.1.0 points to exactly one JAR in Maven Central. No ambiguity. Two companies can both have an artifact named utils as long as their groupIds differ.

In pom.xml you write them as XML elements inside a dependency block. Maven uses these to construct the file path in the repository: ~/.m2/repository/org/springframework/spring-web/6.1.0/spring-web-6.1.0.jar. That's the exact file it downloads and caches.

candidates miss: groupId and package naming follow the same reversed-domain convention but they're independent. Your groupId can be com.example and your main package can also be com.example — or they can differ. They're not required to match.

sections.cap: GAV is the addressing system for every Java artifact. Get comfortable reading and writing these three elements — they're in every dependency block you'll ever touch.

questions.question: What is the difference between a SNAPSHOT version and a release version in Maven?
questions.title: SNAPSHOT vs Release Versions in Maven
questions.direct_answer: A SNAPSHOT version (e.g., 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT) is a work-in-progress build that may change at any time; a release version (e.g., 1.0.0) is immutable and permanently represents that exact state of the code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Maven versioning conventions — SNAPSHOT is a common source of confusion
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Maven re-downloads SNAPSHOTs on every build (if configured) but release versions are cached forever
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that production deployments should never use SNAPSHOT versions — SNAPSHOTs are non-reproducible builds

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven distinguishes between two types of versions. A SNAPSHOT version — like '1.0.0-SNAPSHOT' — is explicitly marked as work in progress. It means 'this is our current development version and it may change at any moment.' Maven treats SNAPSHOTs specially: it periodically checks for updates and can download a newer build of the same SNAPSHOT version. If your team is sharing a SNAPSHOT library between projects, each new build of that library updates the SNAPSHOT and dependents can pick it up. A release version — like '1.0.0' — is immutable by convention. Once you release '1.0.0', that JAR is frozen. Maven caches it in your local repository forever and never checks for updates, because release versions should never change. There's a critical rule: never use SNAPSHOT dependencies in production builds. A production build must be reproducible — you need to know exactly what code you deployed. If you depend on a SNAPSHOT, the library can change between when you tested and when you deployed, making the build non-reproducible and potentially unstable.

sections.title: Key Points
content: SNAPSHOT (e.g., 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT): work in progress, may change, Maven may re-download
Release (e.g., 1.0.0): immutable, Maven caches forever and never re-downloads
SNAPSHOT = mutable development artifact; Release = frozen production artifact
Production builds must use release versions only — SNAPSHOTs break reproducibility
CI/CD typically runs: SNAPSHOT builds during development, then releases before deployment

sections.hook: One version string is frozen forever. The other can change without warning. Knowing which is which matters enormously for production.

beats.content: SNAPSHOT means 'this is the current state of development.' It's designed for team collaboration during active work. Your CI builds a new SNAPSHOT, pushes it to Nexus, and other projects pick it up automatically on their next build.
Release versions are immutable by contract. Once 1.0.0 is published, it should never change. Maven caches it locally forever and trusts that the cached copy is always correct.

production trap: a production build that depends on a SNAPSHOT is non-reproducible. The library could change between your test run and your release deployment. CI/CD gates should reject SNAPSHOT dependencies in release builds.

sections.cap: SNAPSHOT for active development, release for deployment. Never ship SNAPSHOT to production — reproducibility is non-negotiable.

questions.question: What is the standard Maven project directory structure?
questions.title: Maven Standard Directory Structure
questions.direct_answer: Maven's standard structure puts Java source in src/main/java, test source in src/test/java, resources in src/main/resources and src/test/resources, and outputs compiled/packaged artifacts to the target/ directory.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Maven knowledge — a Spring Initializr project follows this structure automatically
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing where to put resources (application.properties) vs source code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the Spring Initializr generates this structure automatically and where application.properties lives

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven's standard structure is straightforward once you know it, and it's what you'll see in every Spring Boot project generated by Spring Initializr. At the root level you have pom.xml — Maven's configuration and dependency file. Then the src directory which splits into main and test. Under src/main/java goes all your production Java source code — your packages and classes. Under src/main/resources goes non-Java files that should be in the classpath at runtime: application.properties, application.yml, logging config, static files. Under src/test/java goes your JUnit test classes. Under src/test/resources goes test-specific resource files, like a test application.properties with an in-memory H2 database config. Maven compiles everything and puts the outputs in the target/ directory — compiled classes go to target/classes, test classes to target/test-classes, and the final JAR or WAR to target/. The target/ directory is always in .gitignore because it's generated output. The entire project can be rebuilt from source code plus pom.xml at any time.

sections.title: Key Points
content: src/main/java: production Java source code
src/main/resources: runtime resources — application.properties, application.yml, templates
src/test/java: JUnit test classes
src/test/resources: test-specific resources (test DB config, test fixtures)
target/: generated build output — always in .gitignore; never commit it

sections.hook: Every Spring Boot project from Spring Initializr follows the same layout. Know this structure and you'll feel at home in any Maven project on day one.

beats.label: Standard Maven directory layout:
items: pom.xml — project config and dependency declarations, at project root
src/main/java — all production Java source code
src/main/resources — application.properties, application.yml, templates, static files
src/test/java — JUnit and Mockito test classes
src/test/resources — test-specific config (H2 test database, test fixtures)
target/ — generated output, always gitignored

beats.content: The split between main and test mirrors the compile vs test scope concept. Everything under main goes into the production artifact. Everything under test only exists during the test phase.

candidates miss: application.properties goes in src/main/resources, not src/main/java. Java files are source code. Properties, YAML files, and templates are resources. Maven copies resources into target/classes alongside compiled .class files so they're all on the classpath at runtime.

sections.cap: This layout is Maven's convention. Follow it and you get zero configuration. Spring Initializr generates it automatically, so you'll see it in every new project.

questions.question: What is Maven Central and how does Maven use it?
questions.title: Maven Central Repository
questions.direct_answer: Maven Central is the default public repository at search.maven.org containing virtually every open-source Java library — Maven automatically downloads declared dependencies from here if they're not already in the local cache.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of where Java dependencies actually come from
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Maven always downloads from the internet — the local cache (~/m2) is checked first
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that publishing to Maven Central requires Sonatype OSS Hosting and GPG signing for security verification

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven Central is the default public repository for Java artifacts, hosted at search.maven.org and repo1.maven.org. When you declare a dependency in pom.xml like Spring Boot or Jackson, Maven first checks your local ~/.m2 cache. If the JAR isn't there, Maven goes to Maven Central to download it and cache it locally. Maven Central hosts hundreds of thousands of open-source Java libraries — virtually everything you'd want is there. It's the npm registry equivalent for Java. One important security feature: artifacts on Maven Central are signed with PGP/GPG keys, and Maven can verify these signatures to ensure you're getting the genuine artifact and not a tampered version. For enterprise environments, companies often set up a proxy like Nexus or Artifactory in front of Maven Central. This acts as a company-wide cache (so if 50 developers need the same dependency, only one download happens), and it lets security teams scan and whitelist/blacklist specific dependencies. You can also search Maven Central directly at search.maven.org to find the right GAV coordinates for any library you want to use.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Maven Central: default public repository at search.maven.org — hosts virtually all open-source Java libs
Resolution: Maven checks local ~/.m2 cache first, then Maven Central
Artifacts are PGP-signed for security verification
search.maven.org: use this to find GAV coordinates for any library
Enterprise: Nexus/Artifactory acts as company proxy/cache in front of Maven Central

sections.hook: Maven Central is the npm registry of the Java world. Every open-source Java library lives there, and Maven knows how to find it using just a GAV coordinate.

beats.content: Maven Central lives at search.maven.org and repo1.maven.org. It hosts hundreds of thousands of open-source Java libraries. When you declare a dependency, Maven checks your local ~/.m2 cache first. Cache miss? It fetches from Maven Central and caches it locally. That first build after a fresh clone is slow. Every build after that is fast.
Artifacts on Maven Central are PGP-signed. Maven can verify those signatures to confirm the JAR hasn't been tampered with. This is why Maven Central is trusted for open-source dependencies.

In enterprise environments you'll rarely hit Maven Central directly. Instead, your network routes through a Nexus or Artifactory proxy. That proxy caches libraries company-wide and lets the security team audit or block specific artifacts.

non-obvious: search.maven.org is also where you find GAV coordinates. Search for a library by name, find the right artifact, click it, and copy the pom.xml snippet directly. Much faster than guessing coordinates.

sections.cap: Maven Central is the default source of truth for Java dependencies. Your local .m2 cache is its mirror on your machine. Nexus/Artifactory is its enterprise-grade proxy.
